title: Friends in good times
hookLine: everyone is a companion in pleasure; in trouble, few remain (Sorath M9, ang 634)

lines: A PROMOTION: THE CHAT LIGHTS UP.
A LOSS: THE CHAT GOES QUIET.
cards: When someone gets a promotion, the group chat lights up. Congratulations, drinks on you, so proud of you, a row of party emojis. When the same person loses the job six months later, the chat goes quiet.
A couple of people send a private message. Most say nothing, not out of cruelty, but because they don't know what to say, and it's easier to look away.
Guru Tegh Bahadur saw it too, long before group chats, and put it in a hymn.

teach.h: NO ONE TRULY BELONGS TO ANYONE.
teach.b: The hymn in Raag Sorath begins, in paraphrase: friend, understand this in your mind. The world is bound up in its own comfort; no one truly belongs to anyone.
In good times, many come and sit with you, crowding round on every side.
When trouble falls, they all leave your company, and no one comes near. Sukh is comfort, good times. Bipat is trouble, calamity.
The hymn's line runs between those two words. Then it goes further than most of us would dare. Even the one at home who loved you most, it says, when the soul leaves the body, runs away crying ghost.
It's a hard sentence, and it's meant to be. The point isn't that people are wicked. It's that human love, left to itself, is tangled up with what we get from each other.
The hymn ends: at the last, says Nanak, nothing helps except the Lord. Yet it doesn't tell you to become bitter.
If everyone drifts off when trouble comes, the one who stays is rare, and Sikh tradition prizes that rarity.
Look at the sangat that turns up with food when someone dies, sitting with the family for days while the Guru Granth Sahib is read.
That's a whole community built to stay. The hymn describes how the world tends to drift away. The practice asks you to be the exception.

how: When a Sikh family loses someone, the sangat often gathers at the home with food and support while a reading of the Guru Granth Sahib is held, and Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymns and saloks are commonly heard at that time.

o: comfort, the good times in life
a promise kept to a friend

games.q: friends in good times — tap the pairs.

s: the hymn tells us to become bitter about friends
it describes the world's way; the practice asks you to be the one who stays.
the hymn says the world is bound up in its own comfort
no one truly belongs to anyone, it says.
the hymn says even the closest ones run away when the soul leaves the body
it's a hard line, meant to show how tangled human love is.

games.q: in the Sorath hymn, trouble falls on someone who had many friends. what do the friends do?
o: leave, and no one comes near.
games.why: in good times many sit round on every side; when trouble falls, they all leave, and no one comes near. at the last, says Nanak, only the Lord helps.

practice: Let one name come to mind, someone going through something hard right now, an illness, a breakup, a lost job, a long grief, and notice if part of you has been keeping away, not sure what to say.
Choose one way to come near, a message, a visit, a meal left at the door, a call where you mostly listen; you don't need wise words, only to show up. If you pray, you can hold them before Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Preet, love. Guru Tegh Bahadur's Sorath hymn looks honestly at how much of our love is tied to our own comfort: many sit with us in sukh, good times, and few come near in bipat, trouble.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: preet, love. The hymn looks honestly at how much of our preet is tied to our own comfort.

carryVoice: Your line: stay in hard times. Two lines in a message can be enough. Five hundred eighty-three days now.

sources.ref: Raag Sorath, Mahalla 9, 'preetam jaan lehu man maahee' (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 634)
